discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Upper level low well offshore will move move southeast and weaken today and tonight. The low will move inland over Oregon Thursday. Front associated with the low moving into Southwest Washington later today and tonight. The front will dissipate late tonight. Upper level ridge building offshore Thursday afternoon will move over Western Washington Thursday night and Friday. Another upper level low will develop off the Oregon coast over the weekend. That low will dissipate Monday. An organized front will reach the area Tuesday.
hydrology: No river flooding expected in the next 7 days.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Upper level low well offshore will move move southeast and weaken today and tonight. The low will move inland over Oregon Thursday. Front associated with the low moving into Southwest Washington later today and tonight. The front will dissipate late tonight. Upper level ridge building offshore Thursday afternoon will move over Western Washington Thursday night and Friday. Another upper level low will develop off the Oregon coast over the weekend. That low will dissipate Monday. An organized front will reach the area Tuesday.

sections.title: Short term (today through Friday)
paragraphs: The latest forecast remains on track this morning with no updates. Upper level low moving southeast today ending up off the Central Oregon coast late this afternoon. Low level offshore flow with the cross cascade gradient bottoming out around -8 mb this morning. This will produce some breezy easterly winds in the foothills into the afternoon hours. Weakening front associated with the low moving into Southwest Washington late in the day. Reports of light rain as far north as Salem and Tillamook with ceilings in the 7000 to 9000 foot range early this morning. These conditions will make their way into Western Washington with the light rain chances as far north as around Everett by late afternoon. Any rain that does reach the surface will be light, just a few hundredths. With the cloudy skies highs will be pretty uniform, near 50.

Low not moving much tonight with what is left of the front dissipating over the southern portion of the area. Chance for light rain from about Everett southward in the evening hours. Lows in the lower 30s to lower 40s.

Weak upper level low remaining over Western Oregon Thursday. Like we saw Monday night into early Tuesday with the upper level low in the vicinity you can't totally rule out showers but most of the area will be dry Thursday. Cloud cover thinning out enough overnight for areas of fog to develop over the Southwest Interior and local river valleys in the morning. The fog will be gone by afternoon. Highs again near 50.

Upper level ridge building offshore Thursday afternoon will move over Western Washington Thursday night into Friday. Dry north northeasterly flow aloft over the area will clear skies out. Another round of morning fog Friday. With the clear skies freezing fog developing over the Southwest Interior early Friday morning. Fog dissipating by afternoon. Under sunny skies highs again near 50. Lows Friday morning in the upper 20s and 30s.
Felton

sections.title: Long term (Friday night through Tuesday)
paragraphs: Extended models in a little bit better agreement this morning with the upper level ridge getting pinched off over the area Friday night and another upper level low stalling off the Oregon coast for the weekend. Bands of moisture spinning around the upper level low moving towards Western Washington. The placement of where the low stalls will be crucial to the weekend forecast. Right now a majority of the ensembles keep the low west of 130W. This will mean just glancing blows for Western Washington from the moisture bands spinning around the low. If the low ends up inside 130W much better chance for showers over the weekend. Models also in good agreement that the low dissipates Monday and an organized, but negatively tilted front, arrives Tuesday. For the most part staying with chance pops for the Saturday through Monday period with likely or higher pops Tuesday with the front.

Snow levels around 2500 feet over the weekend so snow on all the passes if the Cascades get any precipitation. Snow levels rising to 3000 to 4000 feet Monday night and Tuesday. The orientation of the front Tuesday will produce easterly winds in the passes which could trap some cool air near the surface in the passes even though the snow level might be above the pass level.
Highs in the mid 40s to lower 50s with lows in the 30s through the period.
Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Terminals VFR this morning as a low pressure system spins offshore. High clouds will continue to fill in overhead. Lower clouds will start to move in later this afternoon, with the latest guidance keeping the best chances for MVFR (50-60%) in the south interior southward. Ceilings will gradually improve this evening. Rain will start moving in along the coast after 11Z from the south and fill into the interior terminals throughout the day, with most of the rain activity focused south of BLI. Reduced visibility to 4SM possible in rain. NE winds generally 6-8 kt. Locally enhanced easterly winds through the Cascade gaps, Strait of Juan de Fuca, and near HQM with gusts 20-25 kt, decreasing into the afternoon hours. Some of the east winds aloft may reach in the interior for brief low level wind sheer as the front moves through.

KSEA...VFR this morning. Cloud cover will continue to fill in this morning over the terminal. Latest guidance drops the chance of MVFR to 10% for the terminal this afternoon with the rain moving through. NE winds 7-9 kt today will ease late tonight to 5-6 kt.
29/HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system spinning offshore continues to bring elevated seas and winds to the coastal waters. A Gale Warning remains in effect for the outer coastal waters and Small Craft Advisory for the inner coastal waters and West and Central Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas will build this morning to 10-14 feet, then decrease below 10 feet on Thursday. Grays Harbor Bar is now included in a Small Craft Advisory as seas look to build just above 10 feet. As the low pressure system continues its southeasterly trajectory into Oregon, weak high pressure will build over area waters on Thursday and Friday for benign marine conditions. Seas will decrease below 10 feet and winds will remain below advisory criteria.

The pattern will become more active starting this weekend and will continue into next week. A low pressure system offshore dropping from the Gulf of Alaska and clip area waters this weekend, which will bring elevated seas and winds. At this time, latest guidance suggests there is a 70% chance or higher for small craft advisory winds over the coastal waters and a 50-60% through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Seas expected to build 10-13 feet. A stronger system is set to impact the waters Monday and Tuesday. NBM guidance suggests a 70% or higher for gale winds across the coastal waters and a moderate (50-65% chance) of gales through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Additionally, guidance is also hinting a 25-35% chance for storm force gusts across the coastal waters. Seas look to build 12- 16 feet.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: A frontal system will bring periods of rain and mountain snow through today, followed by a brief stretch of dry weather late in the week. Another system is expected to approach the Pacific Northwest this weekend, though its eventual track and associated impacts remain uncertain.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A frontal system will bring periods of rain and mountain snow through today, followed by a brief stretch of dry weather late in the week. Another system is expected to approach the Pacific Northwest this weekend, though its eventual track and associated impacts remain uncertain.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Tuesday...The primary forecast concern early this morning is the passage of an offshore low and its associated frontal system. The warm front has been spreading precipitation inland overnight into this morning, with the cold front following closely behind. As the system moves through today, the more organized precipitation will give way to scattered, post-frontal showers. Snow levels generally ranging from 2500 to 3500 ft will support some light accumulation across the Cascades, with the highest probabilities focused near the Cascade passes. From now until 4 AM Thursday, probabilities for at least 1 inch of snow are 50-80% at the passes, with the higher chances across the southern Cascades. More substantial accumulations remain unlikely, with probabilities for 3 inches or more generally only 5-10%. Snow potential in the Coast Range is considerably lower, with just 10-25% chance of a trace at the highest elevations.

The Hood River Valley remains a more challenging part of the forecast given the potential for east winds to transport cooler, drier air in the area. This could lower temperatures enough to support a rain/snow mix or light snow, particularly at higher elevations. Around Parkdale, probabilities for at least 0.1 inch of snow are 40-60%. Farther down the valley, including Hood River proper and Odell, accumulating snow remains unlikely, with probabilities of 10% or less. Overall, cold rain remains the more probable outcome at these lower elevations.

In addition to the precipitation, a tightening offshore pressure gradient will maintain east winds across the Cascades and through the Columbia River Gorge. The strongest winds are expected during the overnight and early morning hours as the surface low approaches the coast, with the pressure gradient reaching near -5 mb. Gusts of 30-40 mph are possible across the western Columbia River Gorge and far eastern portions of the Portland/Vancouver metro area, with locally stronger gusts in the usual gap-wind-prone locations near the Gorge and adjacent higher terrain.

Conditions should improve fairly quickly following the departure of the system. Ensemble guidance shows strong agreement in developing a narrow ridge along the West Coast, supporting a dry period tonight through much of Friday. The combination of light winds and lingering low-level moisture will favor nocturnal cooling and could result in areas of radiation fog across sheltered valleys during the Thursday and Friday morning commutes.

The next meaningful chance in the pattern is expected late Friday into the weekend, as another trough moves toward the West Coast from the Gulf of Alaska. At this lead time, the latest ensemble clusters show significant spread in both timing and offshore trajectory of the system rather than a single dominant solution. Around 75% of ensemble members favor a more progressive trough digging toward the Oregon and Northern California coast late Friday, which would focus the heaviest precipitation near or south of Cape Blanco. Meanwhile, roughly 25% of members depict a deeper, slower-moving offshore trough that could pull heavier precipitation farther north into Oregon. Depending on how close the surface low tracks to the coast, locally gusty winds may accompany the front, through the probability of gusts exceeding 50 mph remains low (under 10%). ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Thursday...High to mid clouds, rain, and VFR conditions continue over the airspace as of 12Z Wed. Rain will remain light and northward as the front passes through. Chances for MVFR CIGs increase to around 30-50% towards 14-17Z Wed. Conditions then trend back towards VFR around 20-24Z Wed as the rain diminishes. Gusty easterly winds have developed at KPDX and KTTD overnight, of which will continue to bring gusts up to 25 kt at KPDX and KTTD through this afternoon, then weakening into the late afternoon and evening. As for other terminals, expect winds generally under 10 kt, elevated this morning and then becoming light in the late afternoon.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Currently VFR conditions, light rain, and gusty easterly winds. Expect mostly VFR conditions through the TAF period, with the exception of a 30-40% chance of MVFR CIGs from 15Z Wed to 02Z Thu. Rain will also dissipate around 02Z Thu. Gusty easterly winds with gusts up to 25 kt will weaken by 18-21Z Wed. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds continue to weaken this morning, but seas remain elevated around 12-16 ft at 14 seconds due to a fresh westerly swell. As a result of weakened winds, the Gale Warning over the outer waters have been expired and a Hazardous Seas Warning has taken its place through tonight. Small Craft conditions are expected continue for the inner waters and Columbia River Bar through tonight as well. Beyond tonight, it looks like Hazardous Seas conditions will come to an end, resulting in all the waters continuing to have Small Craft conditions through Thursday morning. As a result, a Small Craft Advisory over all the waters has been issued from tonight into Thursday morning.

Calmer conditions arrive Thursday afternoon with seas finally falling below 10 ft and relatively light offshore winds. However, conditions look to ramp up once again for the weekend as yet another system moves towards the coast, bringing southerly winds with gusts up to 40 kt and seas building towards 14-16 ft. ~12/42
